name: Council of Clermont
region: Clermont, city of Auvergne, in the kingdom of the Franks
teaser: Clermont, 1095. Pope Urban II and many bishops and abbots of Gaul decreed that the journey to free the church of Jerusalem, made for devotion alone, would count in place of all penance, and set a truce; nobles sewed the cross onto their clothes.
knownFor: The council at which Urban II called the armed journey to Jerusalem, and Adhémar of Le Puy knelt to ask leave to go, by the account of Baldric, who watched.
datesNote: November 1095, the month William of Tyre gives. Lambert of Saint-Omer has the council sit on 18 November, in a year he gives as 1096. The council was still sitting at the end of the month: a letter of Urban II for the church of Grenoble is dated at Clermont on 29 November, and the act of concord between Cluny and La Chaise-Dieu on 1 December 1095. No source among ours gives the day of Urban's speech
issue: In Baldric's telling, Urban spoke of the troubles of "Christiani nostri fratres" in Jerusalem, Antioch and the other cities of the East, beaten, oppressed and wronged, and called the knights to fight for Jerusalem. Baldric gives the pope's words, or words like them, in his own Latin.

William of Tyre says Urban held a council at Piacenza and then, fleeing the anger of the emperor Henry IV, left Italy and crossed the Alps into the kingdom of the Franks. There he saw faith perished and the rule of the prince of darkness spread far and wide.

William and Albert of Aachen say Peter the Hermit had brought Urban letters from the patriarch of Jerusalem about the sufferings of the Christians there. In William's telling the patriarch told Peter there was no hope from the Greeks, who had lost more than half their empire.

The Book of the Popes says Urban had heard that his predecessor Gregory VII had preached the journey to Jerusalem for the defense of the Christian faith, and could not carry it out because King Henry persecuted him.

The Eastern writers explain the Franks' coming without the council. Anna Komnene says Peter, back from a failed pilgrimage and ill-treated by Turks and Saracens, proclaimed in all the Latin lands that a divine voice bade him call the counts of Frankia to free Jerusalem. Ibn al-Athir says a Frankish prince offered Roger of Sicily help against Africa and Roger pointed them to Jerusalem instead; others, he says, hold that the caliphs of Egypt invited them. Matthew of Edessa sees the prophecy of Saint Nerses fulfilled.
The other side in the West, the emperor Henry IV and his party, has no voice on Clermont in any line among our sources.
Other business came before the council. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, brought his long quarrel with the archbishop of Vienne over the district of Salmorenc (Hugh's own account).
calledBy: Pope Urban II. His own letter to Grenoble speaks of the council which we held at Clermont, city of Auvergne. William of Tyre says Urban first planned a general council at Vézelay, then at Le Puy, before it met at Clermont; Albert of Aachen says he decreed it at Le Puy and then went on to Clermont. The Old French translation of William has it sit at all three places, where the Latin says only that he planned the first two
attended: Baldric, who was there, gives many bishops and abbots of Gaul, and powerful and honored men without number from many regions. William of Tyre gives bishops and abbots from all the provinces beyond the Alps, with some princes; Albert gives the bishops of all France, dukes, counts and great princes.
Lambert, a canon of Saint-Omer, counts 310 bishops, with the pope presiding (his notice of Urban II, printed by Louis Duchesne). No list of names is among our sources.

Named as present: Adhémar, bishop of Le Puy (Baldric, William); William, bishop of Orange (William); Hugh, bishop of Grenoble (his own account); Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Pontius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, with Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges (the act of 1 December); and Baldric himself, then abbot of Bourgueil, who writes "nobis videntibus", while we watched.
Peter the Hermit is present only in William's telling, where Urban calls him "qui praesens est". Baldric does not name him at the council.
decided: The acts are not among our sources. Canons reach us in later copies: two as extracts printed by Carl Mirbt, and others recited again at the council of Beauvais in 1114, printed by Mansi.
Canon 2: whoever sets out to free the church of God at Jerusalem for devotion alone, and not to gain honor or money, shall have that journey counted in place of all penance.

Canon 9, from the Codex of Cencius: because many regions of Gaul were short of food, the truce was to hold without a break for three years for peasants and merchants; for knights from Thursday to Sunday every week; for clerics and monks at all times; and above all for pilgrims going to the holy places.

From the Beauvais record: kings and princes were forbidden to grant investiture of church offices; no layman was to seize another's inheritance, and no priest was to admit him to penance until he made it good; sons of concubines and of clergy were not to be ordained unless they became monks or regular clergy; no cleric was to hold prebends in two cities.

The cross: in Baldric's telling, Urban told those who would go to fit the cross to their clothes, so that they might go more safely and be an example to those who saw them. William says it was laid on them by the pope's command to wear it on their shoulders.
Adhémar: Baldric says he won leave and a blessing to go, and an order from the pope that all should obey him.

In William's version of the speech, Urban relaxes the penances laid on those who take up arms for the pilgrimage, takes their persons and goods under the church's protection, and has anyone who harms them excommunicated by the local bishop until he restores what he took. Bishops and priests who do not resist such men are suspended. This is William's speech, not the acts.
The bishops were told to preach the journey in their own churches (Baldric, William). William adds canons for the reform of morals, and canons of peace made at Peter the Hermit's prompting.

The Grenoble case: Urban's letter, dated at Clermont on 29 November, says the quarrel over Salmorenc was settled by the council's authority in Hugh's favor. Clergy and laity there were forbidden to obey the archbishop of Vienne until the judgment was carried out or the case was settled before the pope.

Cluny and La Chaise-Dieu: a concord between Abbot Hugh and Abbot Pontius over their churches and monks was made at the council by the pope's hand, enacted publicly at Clermont and confirmed by Urban on 1 December 1095.
outcome: While the council sat, Baldric says, envoys of Raymond, count of Toulouse, arrived without warning and bore witness that he had already taken the cross. Those who had been faint-hearted the day before took courage.

The council was dissolved, Baldric writes, and "nos unusquisque properantes redivimus ad propria", each of us hurried home. The bishops preached, lay people shouted it, and every day the number bound for Jerusalem grew.

William of Tyre says the bishops went home and worked, by the synod's statutes, to keep the truce unbroken. He lists princes who took the cross, among them Hugh the Great, Robert of Flanders, Robert of Normandy, Stephen of Blois, Raymond of Toulouse and Godfrey of Lorraine.
Walter of Thérouanne writes that Count Robert of Flanders, son of Robert the Frisian, heard the decree of the council of Clermont and left his wife and children for the journey.
The Book of the Popes says the crowds wanted Urban to go with them, and the whole church would not let him. With his blessing and the absolution of their sins they fought under him and blessed Peter.

Anna Komnene, daughter of the emperor Alexios, says her father heard of countless Frankish armies coming and feared them. The greed and the easy breaking of agreements are her own charges against the Franks. She tells of an unarmed crowd with crosses on their shoulders, women and children among them, like rivers flowing together from everywhere. She names no pope and no council.

Ibn al-Athir says the emperor refused the Franks passage at Constantinople unless they swore to hand Antioch over to him, and they agreed. Matthew of Edessa, an Armenian, says the peoples of Italy and Spain and the farthest nations of the Franks came to free Jerusalem. Neither names the pope or the council.

Étienne Baluze, in his notes to the Lateran council of 1123 printed by Mansi, says the same remission of sins was later granted to those going to fight in Spain as had been granted at Clermont to the defenders of the Eastern church.

traditions.name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
traditions.note: Urban II held the council with many bishops and abbots of Gaul (Baldric), from all the provinces beyond the Alps (William of Tyre).

traditions.name: Cluniac Reform Monasticism
traditions.note: Abbot Hugh of Cluny made a concord with La Chaise-Dieu at the council, by the pope's hand, confirmed on 1 December 1095.

traditions.name: The Latin Church of Outremer
traditions.note: Princes who took the cross after the council went on to Jerusalem (William of Tyre). The crusaders made Bernard of Valence, who had come as Adhémar's chaplain, patriarch of Antioch (Dulaurier's note to Matthew of Edessa).

traditions.name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
traditions.note: Alexios received the Frankish armies and made them swear to hand over Antioch (Ibn al-Athir); Anna Komnene says he feared them.

uncertain: The acts are not among our sources; canons reach us only in later copies, in Mirbt's sourcebook and the Beauvais record of 1114. The fullest account from inside the council is Baldric's, a partisan of the call, who gives Urban's words, or words like them, in his own Latin.
The speech: Baldric, who was there, and William of Tyre, writing about ninety years later, give different speeches. Neither is a record of Urban's words.
The count: Lambert of Saint-Omer gives 310 bishops. Baldric and William give no number, and no list of names is held.

The day: Lambert of Saint-Omer has the council sit on 18 November. William of Tyre gives November, and documents are dated at Clermont on 29 November and 1 December. No source among ours gives the day of the speech.

The year: the act of concord dates itself 1095, and William gives 1095. Lambert of Saint-Omer, writing about 1120 by Duchesne's dating, gives 1096. Migne's heading to the act gives 1096, and the Bollandists give 1095 in one note and 1096 in another. Baldric's printed text says the synod was held the year after a star-shower of April 1095, with "1096" set in brackets, likely an editor's addition.

Who started it: Peter the Hermit and the patriarch's letter (William, Albert); Gregory VII's earlier plan (the Book of the Popes); Peter alone (Anna Komnene); a Frankish prince and Roger of Sicily, or the caliphs of Egypt (Ibn al-Athir); prophecy (Matthew of Edessa).
Whether Peter the Hermit was at the council: William of Tyre says so; Baldric, who was there, does not name him.
Whether Alexios asked the West for help before Clermont, at Piacenza: no line among our sources tells it.

Peter, bishop of Pamplona, is placed at the council only by a Bollandist editor. That Clermont prescribed the Hours of the Virgin for clergy rests on Ruinart, who reports it as hearsay, and on Labbe's printed councils, which the editor of Bruno's Acta cites and accepts. He doubts only the Carthusian vision told beside it. No witness of the time among ours says so.
